title: MCP — check what stuck
intro: Nine self-check questions written from the course notes (this course has no official graded quiz).

choices: An open protocol standardizing how LLM applications connect to tools and data sources
A Python library for calling the Anthropic API
A replacement for REST APIs in web development
A model architecture for faster inference
questions.explanation: The course's analogy: REST standardized web↔backend, LSP standardized IDE↔language tools, MCP standardizes AI apps↔external systems.

questions.prompt: The problem MCP solves is often summarized as…
choices: M×N → M+N: every app no longer needs custom glue for every data source
Making models smaller
Eliminating the need for tool use
Replacing JSON with a binary format
questions.explanation: Without MCP each of M apps builds custom integrations to each of N sources. With MCP, each side implements the protocol once — and a server built once is reused by every compatible app.

questions.prompt: In the architecture, the MCP client…
choices: Is a lightweight program exposing capabilities
Lives inside the host and maintains a 1:1 connection with one server
Is the LLM itself
Stores the papers_info.json files
questions.explanation: Hosts (Claude Desktop, IDEs, agents) contain clients; each client speaks the protocol 1:1 with one server. Servers are the lightweight capability programs.

questions.prompt: With FastMCP, a tool's schema comes from…
choices: A JSON schema file you write by hand
The decorated function's type hints and docstring
The server_config.json entry
The inspector
questions.explanation: @mcp.tool() turns a plain function into a protocol-compliant tool — signature + docstring become the schema. Low-level implementations handle ListToolsRequest/CallToolRequest directly.

questions.prompt: The client session ritual, in order, is…
choices: call_tool → list_tools → initialize
initialize → list_tools → call_tool
list_tools → initialize → call_tool
fetch → generate → evaluate
questions.explanation: Connect (for stdio: launch the subprocess), initialize the session, list what's available, then call. The chatbot repeats this per configured server.

questions.prompt: Which is a RESOURCE rather than a tool?
choices: search_papers — queries arXiv and saves results to disk
papers://{topic} — read-only access to already-stored paper info
Sending a message to a channel
Updating a database record
questions.explanation: Resources are read-only, GET-like data addressed by URI — no side effects. search_papers writes files (tool); send/update are actions (tools).

choices: The model can invoke them autonomously mid-conversation
The server author can ship high-quality, well-tested interaction templates users trigger on demand
Clients can avoid calling initialize()
Servers can store conversation history
questions.explanation: Prompts are pre-defined User/Assistant message templates — authored and tested once on the server (the chatbot exposes them as /prompt commands). Tools are the model-initiated primitive.

questions.prompt: The key operational difference between stdio and remote servers is…
choices: stdio servers are launched by their client as a subprocess; remote servers must already be running independently
stdio is faster because it skips JSON
Remote servers cannot expose resources
stdio servers require OAuth 2.1
questions.explanation: Local: the client owns the lifecycle (command + args in config, env-var auth). Remote: independent infrastructure reached by URL (/sse or /mcp/), OAuth 2.1 available since the March 2025 spec.

questions.prompt: A streamable-HTTP server with stateless_http=True is appropriate when…
choices: Requests are simple and independent — no memory of prior interactions needed
A multi-step workflow needs the server to remember the client across requests
The server runs locally
You need the client to launch the server
questions.explanation: Stateless = independent request/response (and easy scaling). Choose stateful when a workflow genuinely needs session memory across calls.
